papers.title: Neuroelectrophysiological correlates of extended cessation of consciousness in advanced meditators: A multimodal EEG and MEG study
papers.abstract: In some contemplative traditions, 'extended cessation' (EC) refers to a state of advanced meditation in which the meditator self-reports intentionally suppressing their own consciousness and re-emerging with a profound sense of clarity and equanimity. Here, we present the first electrophysiological study of EC, in which five meditators underwent concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) recording. EC significantly increased high-frequency global coherence in all five of the participants, yet it did not consistently affect Lempel-Ziv complexity or power across participants. Our results provide preliminary evidence that the neural signatures of EC may be distinct from other states that are characterized by a loss of consciousness, including deep sleep and anesthesia. EC may not be simply 'switching off' consciousness but rather reorganizing the neural dynamics that underlie consciousness.

papers.title: Cognitive tests of pattern separation as sleep-sensitive measures in middle-aged and older adults: An exploratory study
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are considered both a dementia risk factor and symptom. The present research aimed to identify cognitive tests sensitive to objective sleep quantity or quality, focusing on tests designed to evaluate the earliest cognitive changes in dementia. We recruited adults who were 50 years or older and remotely monitored their sleep patterns for 7 consecutive days using wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries. On day 7, participants completed different cognitive tests; the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), the Prodromal Alzheimers and Mild Cognitive Impairment battery from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), taxing pattern separation, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The final sample included 34 participants (mean age: 65.56, SD: 9.57). There were significant correlations between objective sleep quantity and PVT and MST performance. MoCA scores were correlated with performance on CANTAB and MST. Objective sleep quantity predicted MST performance when controlling for age, sex, and education. Tests of pattern separation are sensitive to objective sleep quantity and early cognitive changes associated with dementia. The sensitivity of pattern separation tests to sleep should be evaluated in a larger study, aiming to identify suitable clinical trial outcome measures for sleep-promoting treatments in older adults.

papers.title: Tetradic Dynamics of Dyadic Sensorimotor Coordination: A Multiscale EEG Hyperscanning Study
papers.abstract: How do leader and follower roles shape the brain mechanisms that support coordinated action between people? This question has therapeutic relevance for conditions such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, where the capacity for reciprocal social coordination is a defining vulnerability. Here, we propose a tetradic framework and examine sensorimotor coordination in 16 healthy adult pairs (15 included in EEG analyses) using dual-brain EEG hyperscanning and a 2x2 within-subject design crossing Role (Leader/Follower) and Condition (Mirroring/Matching). Mirroring required resonance with a partner's movement; Matching required its controlled transformation. This contrast was designed to dissociate automatic from controlled coordination. Behaviourally, Mirroring produced a robust Follower reaction-time advantage: pooling an independent behavioural-only cohort (combined N=64) revealed a smaller Leader advantage, consistent with role-dependent attention-inhibition gating. At the neural level, tonic power and significant phasic condition clusters were greater during Matching than Mirroring, while role-dependent phasic clusters suggested an anticipatory sequence around Leader responses and post-response gating and rebound around Follower responses. Information-theoretic decomposition identified Leader-weighted predictive information in frontal and posterior perceptual regions, Follower-specific adaptive information across frontoparietal and sensorimotor cortices, sparse Synergy in lateral occipital, fusiform, and paracentral cortices, and Redundancy linking pars opercularis and lateral occipital cortex. These findings characterize tetradic coordination within dyads as a multiscale, role-asymmetric architecture in which top-down predictive control and bottom-up adaptive regulation are functionally dissociable. The tetradic framework provides an organizing scaffold for this dissociation, and the role-specific signatures it reveals may offer candidate biomarkers for clinical populations in whom interpersonal coordination is disrupted.

papers.title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading
papers.abstract: Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388-800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group x task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229-334 ms and 377-538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618-723 ms interval, and a group x task interaction in the 562-636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508-629 ms and 660-800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

papers.title: Neural categorisation of rhythm in human newborns
papers.abstract: Music is ubiquitous across cultures, and humans engage in social interactions through music from early in life. A cornerstone of these interactions is rhythm categorisation, allowing the sheer diversity of rhythmic inputs to be mapped onto internal rhythm categories. The pervasiveness of certain rhythm categories across cultures suggests that rhythm categorisation may be partially rooted in neurobiological predispositions constraining the internal representations of rhythm. However, this view appears to conflict with the diversity of music practices across cultures, which points to a role of experience in rhythm categorisation. To assess the relative contributions of neurobiological predispositions and experience, we tested 0- to 3-day-old newborns, capitalising on their minimal postnatal experience with music. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we recorded, in newborns and adults, brain responses to drum sounds whose pattern of relative interval duration ranged from isochronous to long-short rhythms (1:1 - 2:1 interval ratio). Results indicate significant categorisation in newborns's neural responses, with a representational structure that correlate with those of adults, yet with a greater degree of differentiation across rhythms. These findings reveal neurobiological predispositions enabling rhythm categorisation to be present at birth and further shaped across the lifespan, highlighting the evolutionary roots and plasticity supporting this human cultural practice.

papers.title: Multi-parametric spectral modeling disentangles synaptic kinetics and neural excitability from non-invasive electrophysiological recordings
papers.abstract: Spectral modeling of electrophysiological recordings enables non-invasive characterization of neural excitability. However, current approaches rely on a single spectral index, limiting insight into the multiple biophysical processes underlying excitation-inhibition balance. Here, we introduce a biologically informed, multi-parametric spectral analysis that disentangles neural excitability and synaptic kinetics from recordings. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that this approach captures signatures of hyperexcitability and glutamate reuptake dysfunction characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
papers.abstract: The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

papers.title: Cooperative processing of visual threat across collicular pathways
papers.abstract: Rapid defensive actions require the transformation of sensory cues into appropriate motor responses. The superior colliculus is central to this transformation, containing defined cell-types that form parallel output pathways linking visual inputs to distinct behaviors. However, whether these pathways act independently or cooperate remains unclear. Here we combine cell-type-specific inhibition, large-scale electrophysiology, and functional ultrasound imaging to determine how these pathways contribute to visually evoked defensive behaviors. Inhibiting either narrow-field or wide-field neurons impaired escape to overhead visual threats, demonstrating that both pathways contribute to escape. Recordings from downstream targets revealed a compact representation in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus that selectively distinguished visual stimuli associated with escape, whereas the lateral posterior thalamus contained a broader representation of visual stimuli. The representation of visual threat in the deeper layers of the superior colliculus predicted escape initiation and vigor in freely moving animals. Across the brain, functional ultrasound imaging showed that visual stimuli recruited distinct patterns of activity that could not be explained by response magnitude alone or by the contribution of single cell-types. Together, these results reveal a cooperative circuit architecture in which parallel pathways carry distinct but complementary signals that jointly support visually evoked escape.

papers.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
papers.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory. Net excitatory input onto this population decreased, most strongly that from older-memory populations, which allowed inputs of older memories to drive their own neurons again. Spreading the same total synaptic change evenly across all target populations abolished this recovery. We call this mechanism reactivation-targeted pruning: plasticity is confined to one population, whose neurons lose inputs that are silent when they fire. The mechanism held under Dale's law, and depression of excitatory synapses alone, without any inhibitory plasticity, was sufficient. These findings suggest mechanistic principles underlying REM sleep's role in memory consolidation and highlight the potential for integrating human-like learning behaviors into artificial neural networks.

papers.title: A Humanized Mouse Model of DRPLA Recapitulates Epilepsy and Demonstrates Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Disease Modification
papers.abstract: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) is an ultra-rare progressive myoclonus epilepsy caused by a glutamine-coding CAG repeat expansion in atrophin-1 (ATN1). Mutant ATN1 (mATN1) expression results in symptoms that inversely correlate to CAG-expansion size: young-onset cases have the most CAG repeats and developmental delay, high-frequency treatment-resistant seizures, and early mortality. We sought to characterize the seizure susceptibility of a fully humanized ATN1 mouse expressing human mATN1 with 112 CAG repeats to then assess therapeutic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) intervention on seizure-related outcomes. Atn1Q112/+ or wild-type (WT) mice were treated with investigational ASO targeting human, CAG-expanded, ATN1 or saline (P2 and then again at 4 weeks-old) before acute seizure testing, ataxia profiling, and chronic in vivo video-EEG recording for spontaneous seizures up to 8 weeks-old. Saline-treated Atn1Q112/+ mice were more seizure prone with early death. However, ASO administration to Atn1Q112/+ mice normalized seizure threshold, decreased ataxia, and protected against early death. Atn1Q112/+ mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures recorded over 2 weeks, which were absent in ASO-treated Atn1Q112/+ and WT mice, with a specific mATN1 expression-driven decrease in delta and theta EEG frequencies. Atn1Q112/+ mice are highly seizure prone, validating this model for DRPLA epilepsy. ATN1 represents a novel epilepsy-related risk factor for therapeutic investigation.
